track.title: English Speaking
track.tagline: From A1 basics to boardroom confidence

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.summary: Say your name, role and where you are from, clearly and confidently.

sections.b:
Pattern: Hi, I'm + name. I'm a/an + job. I work at/for + company. I'm from + city.
Use 'a' before consonant sounds (a teacher) and 'an' before vowel sounds (an engineer).
First meetings, team calls and interviews all start with an introduction. Keep it to 2-3 sentences and smile.
Say 'I am an engineer', not 'I am engineer'. English needs the article a/an before a job.

lessons.example:
A: Hi, I'm Priya. I'm an analyst at Infosys.
B: Nice to meet you, Priya. I'm Rahul. I work in sales.
A: Nice to meet you too!
speak: Hi, I'm Yash. I'm a finance student from Ahmedabad.
Nice to meet you.
I work in the marketing team.

quiz.why: Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an engineer.

quiz.q: Which is a good short introduction?
options: Hi, I'm Priya. I'm an analyst at Infosys.
I am Priya, I am doing analyst.

lessons.title: Greetings and saying goodbye
lessons.summary: Formal and informal ways to say hello and goodbye.

sections.b:
Formal: Good morning / Good afternoon / Good evening. How do you do?
Informal: Hi! / Hello! / Hey!
Goodbye: Bye! / See you tomorrow. / Have a nice day. / Take care.
With managers and clients, start with 'Good morning' or 'Hello'. With teammates, 'Hi' is fine. End a call with 'Thank you, have a nice day.'
'Good night' is only for going to bed or leaving at night, not a greeting. In the evening say 'Good evening' to greet.

lessons.example:
A: Good morning, Ms Shah. How are you?
B: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
A: Very well, thanks.
speak: Good morning! How are you?
I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Have a nice day. See you tomorrow.

quiz.q: You meet a client at 7 pm. What do you say?
quiz.why: 'Good evening' is a greeting; 'Good night' is a goodbye.

quiz.q: A good reply to 'How are you?' is…
options: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

lessons.title: Numbers, time and dates
lessons.summary: Say times and dates correctly for meetings.

sections.b:
Time: 9:00 = nine o'clock; 9:15 = nine fifteen / quarter past nine; 9:30 = nine thirty / half past nine; 9:45 = quarter to ten.
Dates: on Monday, on 5th March, in March, at 10 am.
Ordinals: 1st first, 2nd second, 3rd third, 21st twenty-first.
Confirm meeting times clearly: 'The meeting is on Tuesday at 3 pm.' Repeat numbers back to avoid mistakes.
Prepositions: AT a time, ON a day/date, IN a month/year. 'On Monday at 10 am in June.'

lessons.example:
A: When is the review?
B: It's on Friday, the 12th, at half past two.
A: Great, Friday at 2:30. Thanks!
speak: The meeting is on Monday at ten o'clock.
My birthday is on the twenty-first of May.
Let's meet at half past three.

quiz.q: Complete: The call is ___ Tuesday ___ 4 pm.
quiz.why: ON for days, AT for times.

lessons.title: Asking simple questions
lessons.summary: Use question words to get information.

sections.b:
Who (person), What (thing), Where (place), When (time), Why (reason), How (way).
With 'be': Where is the meeting room?
With other verbs use do/does: Where do you work? What does she do?
Questions keep conversations going and help you understand tasks: 'When is the deadline?' 'Who is the client?'
Don't say 'Where you work?' Use 'do/does': 'Where do you work?'

lessons.example:
A: What do you do?
B: I'm a designer.
A: Where do you work?
B: At a startup in Pune.
speak: Where do you work?
When is the deadline?
What does your team do?

quiz.why: Use 'does' with he/she/it and the base verb 'work'.

quiz.q: Which word asks about a reason?

lessons.title: Daily routines: present simple
lessons.summary: Talk about habits and routines.

sections.b:
Present simple for routines: I start work at 9. She checks emails every morning. We have a meeting every Monday.
Add -s/-es for he/she/it: work → works, watch → watches.
Frequency words: always, usually, often, sometimes, never (before the main verb).
Describe your workday in interviews and small talk: 'I usually start with emails, then I join the team stand-up.'
Remember the -s: 'He works', not 'He work'.

lessons.example:
A: What's your typical day like?
B: I usually start at nine. I check emails, then I have a stand-up at ten.
speak: I usually start work at nine.
She always checks her emails first.
We have a team meeting every Monday.

quiz.q: Complete: My manager ___ to the office by metro.
Complete: She ___ the reports every Friday.

lessons.title: Magic words: please, thank you, sorry
lessons.summary: Polite basics that make every interaction smoother.

sections.b:
Please: for requests. Thank you / Thanks: for help. Sorry: for mistakes. Excuse me: to get attention or pass by.
Replies: You're welcome. / No problem. / That's okay.
Politeness is expected in corporate English. 'Can you send it, please?' sounds much better than 'Send it.'
Use 'Excuse me' to get someone's attention, and 'Sorry' to apologise. 'Sorry, could you repeat that?' is fine for not hearing.

lessons.example:
A: Excuse me, could you help me with the printer, please?
B: Sure.
A: Thank you so much!
B: You're welcome.
speak: Could you help me, please?
Thank you so much for your help.
Sorry, I'm late.

quiz.why: 'You're welcome' is the standard reply to thanks.

quiz.q: You bump into someone. You say…

lessons.title: Family and people around you
lessons.summary: Talk about your family and the people in your life.

sections.b:
Family words: mother, father, parents, brother, sister, son, daughter, husband, wife, grandparents, cousin.
Patterns: I have two brothers. My sister is a doctor. My parents live in Surat.
Use 'has' with he/she: My brother has a car.
Small talk often includes family. Keep it simple and positive, and ask back: 'Do you have any brothers or sisters?'
Say 'I have two brothers', not 'I am having two brothers'. 'Have' for possession usually isn't used in the continuous form.

lessons.example:
A: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
B: Yes, I have one sister. She's a teacher in Pune. What about you?
A: I'm an only child.
speak: I have one sister and two brothers.
My parents live in Ahmedabad.
Do you have any brothers or sisters?

quiz.q: Complete: My brother ___ a new job.

lessons.title: There is / there are
lessons.summary: Describe what is in a place.

sections.b:
There is + singular: There is a meeting room on the 3rd floor.
There are + plural: There are ten people in my team.
Questions: Is there a canteen? Are there any parking spaces?
Negative: There isn't a lift. There aren't any chairs.
Useful for describing your office, city or a process: 'There are three steps in the approval process.'
Don't say 'It has a canteen in our office.' Say 'There is a canteen in our office.'

lessons.example:
A: Is there a cafeteria in your building?
B: Yes, there is. There are also two meeting rooms on each floor.
speak: There is a meeting room on the third floor.
There are ten people in my team.
Is there a canteen in this building?

quiz.q: Complete: ___ five people in the meeting.

options: Is a gym in my office.
There is a gym in my office.
It has a gym in my office.
There are a gym in my office.
quiz.why: Use 'there is' to say something exists.

lessons.title: Can and can't: abilities
lessons.summary: Say what you can and can't do.

sections.b:
Can + base verb (no 'to'): I can speak Hindi. She can use Excel.
Negative: can't / cannot: I can't drive.
Questions: Can you code in Python? Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
Describing skills in interviews and introductions: 'I can analyse data in Excel and I can speak three languages.'
Never add 'to' after can: 'I can to speak' ✗ → 'I can speak' ✓. And 'he can', not 'he cans'.

lessons.example:
A: Can you use Power BI?
B: Yes, I can. I can also build basic dashboards in Excel.
A: Great!
speak: I can speak English, Hindi and Gujarati.
I can't drive, but I can ride a bike.
Can you help me with this report?

quiz.q: The short answer to 'Can you drive?' (yes) is…
Which describes a skill for an interview?
options: I can analyse data in Excel.

lessons.title: Food and ordering
lessons.summary: Order food politely at a restaurant or canteen.

sections.b:
Ordering: I'd like a coffee, please. / Can I have the paneer sandwich? / I'll have the thali.
Asking: What do you recommend? / Is it spicy? / Can I have the bill, please?
'I'd like' = I would like (polite).
Team lunches and client dinners are common. Polite ordering makes a good impression.
Avoid 'Give me a coffee.' It sounds rude. Use 'Could I have…' or 'I'd like…'

lessons.example:
Waiter: Are you ready to order?
You: Yes, I'd like the veg biryani, please. Is it very spicy?
Waiter: A little.
You: That's fine. And a sweet lassi, please.
speak: I'd like a cup of tea, please.
Is this dish very spicy?
Could we have the bill, please?

options: Could I have some water, please?
quiz.why: Could I have… please is polite.

quiz.q: To ask for the final payment amount at a restaurant, you ask for…
quiz.why: In India and the UK: bill (US: check).

lessons.title: Asking for and giving directions
lessons.summary: Find your way around an office or a new city.

sections.b:
Asking: Excuse me, where is the HR department? / How do I get to the station?
Giving: Go straight. Turn left/right. It's on your left. It's next to the lift. Take the stairs to the second floor.
Visitors and new joiners need directions. Clear, short steps help.
Use 'on the left' / 'on your right', and 'turn left' (no 'to'): 'Turn to left' ✗ → 'Turn left' ✓.

lessons.example:
A: Excuse me, where's the conference room?
B: Go straight, then turn right. It's the second door on your left, next to the pantry.
speak: Excuse me, where is the conference room?
Go straight and turn left.
It's next to the lift on your right.

quiz.q: 'It's next to the lift' means it is…
How do you start politely when asking a stranger?

lessons.title: My, your, his, her: possessives
lessons.summary: Show who something belongs to.

sections.b:
Subject → possessive: I → my, you → your, he → his, she → her, it → its, we → our, they → their.
Also 's: Priya's laptop, the company's office.
Question: Whose bag is this? It's Rahul's.
Talking about ownership and responsibility: 'This is our new project. Her team handles design.'
'Its' (possessive) has no apostrophe. 'It's' means 'it is'. The company changed its logo.

lessons.example:
A: Whose laptop is this?
B: It's Neha's. Her laptop is the silver one.
A: And where's your charger?
B: My charger is in my bag.
speak: This is my manager, and that is her team.
Whose laptop is this?
Our company changed its logo last year.

lessons.title: Likes and dislikes
lessons.summary: Talk about what you enjoy and don't enjoy.

sections.b:
Like/love/enjoy + -ing: I like reading. She loves cooking. I enjoy working in teams.
Dislike: I don't like / I hate waiting.
Ask: What do you like doing at the weekend?
Soften: I'm not a big fan of…
Sharing interests builds rapport with colleagues. Interviewers may ask: 'What do you enjoy about your work?'
'Enjoy' always needs an object or -ing: 'I enjoy.' ✗ → 'I enjoy it.' / 'I enjoy working.' ✓

lessons.example:
A: What do you like doing in your free time?
B: I love playing cricket and I enjoy watching movies. I'm not a big fan of shopping!
speak: I enjoy working with numbers.
What do you like doing at the weekend?
I'm not a big fan of long meetings.

quiz.q: Complete: I enjoy ___ with my team.
Which is a soft way to say you dislike something?
options: I'm not a big fan of it.

lessons.title: What are you doing now? Present continuous
lessons.summary: Describe actions happening now or around now.

sections.b:
am/is/are + -ing: I'm working on the budget. She's attending a meeting. They're travelling this week.
Questions: What are you working on? Are you coming?
Use for now or temporary situations.
Status updates: 'I'm finalising the slides now.' 'We're hiring two analysts this month.'
Don't use present continuous for routines: 'I'm going to the gym every day' ✗ → 'I go to the gym every day' ✓.

lessons.example:
A: Hi, are you free?
B: Sorry, I'm preparing for a client call right now. Can I call you in 30 minutes?
speak: I'm working on the monthly report right now.
What are you working on this week?
She's attending a client meeting at the moment.

quiz.q: Complete: Please wait, I ___ on a call.

options: I go to the office every day.

lessons.title: In, on, under, next to: places
lessons.summary: Say where things are.

sections.b:
in (inside): in the drawer, in the meeting room.
on (surface): on the desk, on the wall.
under, next to, between, behind, in front of, opposite.
Cities/countries: in Mumbai, in India.
Finding files, people and objects: 'The contract is in the blue folder on my desk.'
'In the office' (inside the building) vs 'at the office' (at your workplace location). Both are common: 'I'm at the office today.'

lessons.example:
A: Where's the stapler?
B: It's on the shelf, next to the printer. The paper is in the drawer under it.
speak: The file is on my desk, next to the laptop.
The keys are in the top drawer.
The meeting room is opposite the lift.

quiz.q: Complete: The picture is ___ the wall.

lessons.title: Weather and easy small talk
lessons.summary: Start friendly conversations with simple topics.

sections.b:
It's hot / cold / humid / rainy / sunny / windy today.
It's raining. It's going to rain later.
Questions: How's the weather in Delhi? Is it still raining there?
Weather is a safe opener, especially on calls with people in other cities or countries.
Say 'It's raining' (now) and 'It rains a lot in July' (general). Don't say 'Today is raining.'

lessons.example:
A: How's the weather in London?
B: It's cold and cloudy. What about Mumbai?
A: It's very humid. The monsoon is here!
speak: It's very hot and humid today.
How's the weather there?
It's going to rain this evening.

quiz.why: Lots of moisture in the air.

quiz.q: Why is weather useful in small talk?

lessons.title: Shopping and prices
lessons.summary: Ask about prices and buy things confidently.

sections.b:
How much is this? / How much are these? It's ₹500. They're ₹200 each.
Can I pay by card / UPI? Do you have this in a bigger size? I'll take it.
Numbers: hundred, thousand, lakh (India), million.
Useful for buying office supplies, ordering, and talking about costs with vendors.
Use 'How much is' for singular and 'How much are' for plural. 'How many' is for countable quantities, not prices.

lessons.example:
A: How much are these notebooks?
B: They're ₹80 each.
A: I'll take five. Can I pay by UPI?
B: Sure.
speak: How much is this laptop bag?
Can I pay by UPI?
I'll take two of these, please.

quiz.why: A common way to decide to buy.

lessons.title: Talking about the past
lessons.summary: Use past simple to describe what happened.

sections.b:
Regular verbs add -ed: work → worked, finish → finished.
Common irregulars: go → went, have → had, meet → met, send → sent, make → made.
Questions/negatives use 'did' + base verb: Did you send it? I didn't see it.
Updates and small talk: 'Yesterday I met the client and sent the proposal.' 'How was your weekend? I went to Lonavala.'
After 'did', use the base verb: 'Did you send it?' not 'Did you sent it?'

lessons.example:
A: How was your weekend?
B: Great! I visited my parents and watched a movie. What about you?
speak: I finished the report yesterday.
Did you send the email to the client?
We met the new manager last week.

options: Did you go to the meeting?
Do you went to the meeting?
Did you went to the meeting?
Did you goes to the meeting?

quiz.q: Complete: I ___ see the email yesterday.

lessons.title: Making polite requests
lessons.summary: Ask for help politely using can, could and would.

sections.b:
Can you…? (informal) → Could you…? (polite) → Would you mind + -ing…? (very polite).
Examples: Could you share the file? Would you mind checking this?
Asking permission: Can I / Could I / May I…?
In emails and meetings, 'Could you…' is the safe default. 'Would you mind…' is good with seniors and clients.
'Would you mind' is followed by -ing: 'Would you mind sending…', not 'Would you mind to send…'

lessons.example:
A: Could you send me the slides before the meeting?
B: Sure, I'll send them by noon.
A: Thanks a lot.
speak: Could you share the file with me, please?
Would you mind checking my report?
May I ask a quick question?

options: Would you mind sending the file?
quiz.why: 'Would you mind + -ing' is the most polite.

quiz.q: Complete: Would you mind ___ the door?

lessons.title: Phone and video call basics
lessons.summary: Start, manage and end calls confidently.

sections.b:
Starting: Hello, this is Yash from Finance. Is this a good time?
Problems: Sorry, you're breaking up. / Can you hear me? / You're on mute.
Ending: Thanks for your time. I'll send a summary. Bye!
Video calls are daily work. Clear openings and closings sound professional.
Say 'This is Yash', not 'I am Yash speaking' on the phone.

lessons.example:
A: Hello, this is Yash from Finance. Is this a good time?
B: Yes, go ahead.
A: I'm calling about the invoice from last week.
speak: Hello, this is Yash from the finance team.
Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you repeat that?
Thanks for your time. I'll send a summary.

quiz.q: How do you introduce yourself on the phone?
quiz.why: 'This is…' is standard on the phone.

quiz.q: 'Is this a good time?' is used to…
options: Check if the person can talk

lessons.title: Describing your job and company
lessons.summary: Explain what you do and what your company does.

sections.b:
I'm responsible for + noun/-ing: I'm responsible for client reports.
I work on + project. I report to + manager. My company provides/makes/sells…
Our team handles…
Useful in interviews, networking and introductions with new teams.
'Responsible for' + -ing: 'responsible for preparing', not 'responsible to prepare'.

lessons.example: I'm a financial analyst at a fintech company. I'm responsible for preparing monthly reports, and I report to the CFO. Our company provides digital payment solutions.
speak: I'm responsible for preparing monthly reports.
I report to the head of finance.
Our company provides digital payment solutions.

quiz.q: Complete: I'm responsible ___ managing the budget.
Which describes what a company does?

lessons.title: Talking about plans and the future
lessons.summary: Use 'going to', 'will' and present continuous for the future.

sections.b:
Going to: plans already decided. I'm going to apply for the role.
Will: quick decisions, promises, predictions. I'll call you back.
Present continuous: arranged events. I'm meeting the client tomorrow.
Commitments: 'I'll send it today.' Plans: 'We're going to launch next month.'
Use 'will' for decisions made at the moment of speaking: 'The phone's ringing.' 'I'll get it.'

lessons.example:
A: What are your plans for next quarter?
B: We're going to expand to Bangalore, and I'm meeting the vendor on Monday.
speak: I'll send you the details today.
We're going to launch the product next month.
I'm meeting the client tomorrow morning.

quiz.q: Your manager asks for the file. You decide now: 'Sure, I ___ send it.'

options: Present continuous: I'm meeting him tomorrow.

lessons.title: Asking for clarification
lessons.summary: Never pretend to understand. Ask politely.

sections.b: Sorry, could you repeat that? / Could you speak a bit more slowly? / What do you mean by…? / Just to confirm, you need it by Friday? / Could you spell that, please?
Clarifying saves hours of rework. Confirm deadlines, numbers and names.
Avoid just saying 'What?'. It sounds rude. Use 'Sorry, could you repeat that?'

lessons.example:
A: We need the KPI deck by EOD.
B: Sorry, what do you mean by EOD?
A: End of day.
B: Got it. Just to confirm, today by 6 pm?
speak: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?
What do you mean by that?
Just to confirm, the deadline is Friday?

quiz.q: Which is the most professional way to ask someone to repeat?
'Could you spell that, please?' is useful for…

lessons.title: Comparing things
lessons.summary: Use comparatives and superlatives to compare options.

sections.b:
Short adjectives: cheap → cheaper → the cheapest; fast → faster → the fastest.
Long adjectives: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive.
Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst.
as … as: This plan is as good as that one.
Comparing vendors, tools and options: 'Option B is cheaper but slower. Option C is the most reliable.'
Don't double: 'more cheaper' ✗ → 'cheaper' ✓. Use 'than' after comparatives: 'faster than'.

lessons.example: Vendor A is cheaper than Vendor B, but Vendor B is faster. Vendor C is the most expensive, but it has the best support.
speak: This laptop is lighter than the old one.
Option C is the most reliable choice.
Their service is better than ours.

options: This is more cheap than that.

quiz.q: Complete: This tool is ___ than the old one.

lessons.title: Much, many, some, any
lessons.summary: Talk about quantities correctly.

sections.b:
Countable (can count): meetings, emails, files → many, a few, how many.
Uncountable: information, advice, money, feedback, equipment → much, a little, how much.
Some (positive), any (questions/negatives): We have some time. Do you have any questions?
Very common in work talk: 'How much time do we have?' 'We don't have many resources.'
Information, advice, feedback and equipment are uncountable: 'an advice' ✗ → 'some advice' / 'a piece of advice' ✓. Never 'informations'.

lessons.example:
A: Do you have any feedback on my draft?
B: Yes, some. Not much, just a few small changes.
speak: Do you have any questions?
How much time do we have left?
Can you give me some feedback?

options: Can I give you an advice?
Can I give you some advice?
Can I give you many advice?

quiz.q: Complete: How ___ emails did you get?

lessons.title: Was doing: past continuous
lessons.summary: Describe background actions in the past.

sections.b:
was/were + -ing: I was working when you called. They were having lunch at 1 pm.
Often with past simple: While I was presenting, the projector stopped.
While + continuous; when + simple.
Explaining what happened in incidents and delays: 'We were testing the app when the server crashed.'
Use past continuous for the longer background action and past simple for the short interruption.

lessons.example:
A: Why didn't you answer my call?
B: Sorry, I was presenting to the client. I called you back when I finished.
speak: I was working on the report when you called.
We were testing the app when the server crashed.
What were you doing at ten o'clock?

quiz.q: Complete: I ___ lunch when the client arrived.

options: While I presented, the power was going off.
While I presenting, power went off.
While I am presenting, the power went off.
While I was presenting, the power went off.

quiz.q: Complete: They ___ a meeting at 3 pm yesterday.

lessons.title: Invitations: accept and decline politely
lessons.summary: Invite colleagues and respond graciously.

sections.b:
Invite: Would you like to join us for lunch? / Are you free on Friday evening? / We're having a team dinner. Can you come?
Accept: I'd love to! / Sounds great, thanks.
Decline: Thanks for asking, but I'm afraid I can't. I have another commitment. Maybe next time?
Team bonding matters. A polite decline keeps relationships warm.
'Would you like to' + base verb. Don't just say 'No' when declining: give thanks, a short reason and an alternative.

lessons.example:
A: Would you like to join us for lunch?
B: I'd love to, but I'm afraid I have a call at one. Can we go tomorrow instead?
speak: Would you like to join us for lunch?
I'd love to, thanks for asking!
I'm afraid I can't today. Maybe next time?

options: Thanks, but I'm afraid I can't today.

lessons.title: Giving advice with should
lessons.summary: Recommend and suggest using should, ought to and had better.

sections.b:
should + base verb: You should back up your files. You shouldn't share your password.
ought to (similar, more formal).
had better (stronger, warning): You'd better leave now or you'll miss the train.
Ask: What should I do?
Helping colleagues and juniors: 'You should check the numbers with finance before sending.'
No 'to' after should: 'You should to call' ✗ → 'You should call' ✓.

lessons.example:
A: I'm nervous about my presentation.
B: You should practise it twice out loud. And you shouldn't read from the slides.
speak: You should back up your files every day.
You shouldn't share your password with anyone.
What should I do first?

lessons.title: Describing people
lessons.summary: Describe appearance and personality.

sections.b:
Appearance: tall, short, slim, has short hair, wears glasses.
Personality: friendly, hard-working, reliable, patient, creative, organised.
Questions: What's she like? (personality) / What does she look like? (appearance)
Giving references, describing team members and introducing colleagues: 'Ravi is very reliable and great with clients.'
'What is he like?' asks about personality, not likes. 'What does he like?' asks about his interests.

lessons.example:
A: What's your new manager like?
B: She's very organised and supportive. She's also very patient with new joiners.
speak: My manager is very supportive and organised.
What's your new teammate like?
He's reliable and always meets deadlines.

lessons.title: Leaving a voicemail or message
lessons.summary: Leave clear, short phone and voice messages.

sections.b:
Structure: greeting + name + company → reason → action needed → number/time → thanks.
'Hi Amit, this is Yash from Finance. I'm calling about the invoice for March. Could you call me back today on 98xxxxxx? Thanks!'
Taking messages: Can I take a message? / I'll ask him to call you back.
Voice notes on WhatsApp and voicemails are common. Clear structure saves time.
Say numbers slowly and in groups: 98250 / 12345. Repeat important details.

lessons.example: Hi Meera, this is Yash from the finance team. I'm calling about tomorrow's budget meeting. Could you send me the latest numbers by 5 pm? You can reach me on 98250 12345. Thanks!
speak: Hi, this is Yash from the finance team.
I'm calling about tomorrow's meeting.
Could you call me back on this number? Thanks!

quiz.q: What should come right after your name in a voicemail?
How should you say a phone number?
'Can I take a message?' is said by…
quiz.why: Offering to pass on a message.

lessons.title: Travel and bookings
lessons.summary: Book tickets, hotels and handle travel situations.

sections.b:
Booking: I'd like to book a room for two nights. / Is breakfast included? / What time is check-out?
Transport: A return ticket to Delhi, please. / Which platform does the train leave from? / My flight is delayed.
Problems: There's a problem with my booking. / Could you help me?
Business travel needs confident communication at airports, hotels and with taxis.
'Book' is a verb here: 'I booked a hotel.' 'Reserve' is also fine. Check-in/check-out are nouns or phrasal verbs.

lessons.example:
Hotel: Good evening, how can I help?
You: Hi, I have a booking under the name Modi, for two nights.
Hotel: Yes, Mr Modi. Breakfast is included, and check-out is at 11.
speak: I'd like to book a room for two nights.
Is breakfast included?
My flight is delayed by two hours.

quiz.q: Which question asks about leaving time at a hotel?
Complete: I have a booking ___ the name Shah.

lessons.title: Health and taking sick leave
lessons.summary: Explain how you feel and inform your manager professionally.

sections.b:
I'm not feeling well. I have a headache / fever / cold / stomach ache. I need to see a doctor.
Informing: I'm afraid I won't be able to come in today. I'll be on sick leave. I'll check my messages for anything urgent.
Wishing: Get well soon! Take care.
A short, clear message about sick leave is professional. Include what's covered and who can help.
Say 'I have a fever' (not 'I am having fever'). Avoid too much medical detail at work.

lessons.example: Hi Neha, I'm not feeling well today. I have a fever, so I'll take sick leave. Rohan can help with the client call at 3. I'll check messages for anything urgent. Thanks!
speak: I'm not feeling well today.
I have a fever, so I'll take sick leave.
Get well soon and take care!

quiz.q: What do you say to a colleague who is ill?

lessons.title: Time expressions: ago, last, next
lessons.summary: Place events in time correctly.

sections.b:
Past: two days ago, last week, last Monday, yesterday, in 2022.
Future: next week, next Monday, tomorrow, in two days.
No 'the': last week (not 'the last week' for 'previous'), next month.
Status reports and planning rely on clear time references: 'We launched the app three weeks ago; the next release is next month.'
Use 'ago' with past simple: 'I joined two years ago.' Don't say 'before two years'.

lessons.example: I joined the company two years ago. Last month we launched a new product, and next quarter we're expanding to Hyderabad.
speak: I joined the company two years ago.
We met the client last Tuesday.
The next release is next month.

options: I joined two years before now ago.

quiz.q: Complete: We had the review ___ week.

lessons.title: Apologising properly
lessons.summary: Say sorry sincerely and fix the problem.

sections.b:
Simple: Sorry I'm late. / I'm really sorry about that.
Formal: I apologise for the delay. / Please accept my apologies.
Strong apology = apology + responsibility + fix: I'm sorry, that was my mistake. I'll correct it and send it by 4 pm.
Owning mistakes quickly builds trust. Avoid long excuses.
'Apologise for + noun/-ing': 'I apologise for the delay / for sending the wrong file.' Not 'apologise to the delay'.

lessons.example: I'm really sorry, I sent you last month's file by mistake. That's my error. Here's the correct version, and I've double-checked the numbers.
speak: I'm sorry, that was my mistake.
I apologise for the delay.
I'll fix it and send it by four o'clock.

lessons.title: Giving opinions
lessons.summary: Share your view clearly and support it with a reason.

sections.b:
Opening: I think… / In my opinion… / From my point of view… / I feel that…
Reason: because… / The main reason is… / For example…
Structure: Opinion + reason + example.
In meetings, a structured opinion sounds confident and thoughtful.
Say 'In my opinion', not 'According to me' (common in Indian English but sounds unnatural to many listeners).

lessons.example: In my opinion, we should delay the launch by a week. The main reason is that testing isn't complete. For example, the payment flow still fails on older phones.
speak: In my opinion, we should focus on existing customers.
The main reason is that they bring repeat revenue.
For example, our top ten clients bring forty percent of sales.

options: According to me, it's a good idea.
As per me, it's good idea.
In my opinion, it's a good idea.
quiz.why: 'In my opinion' is standard and natural.

quiz.q: Which is a natural opinion opener?

lessons.title: Agreeing and disagreeing politely
lessons.summary: Disagree without damaging relationships.

sections.b:
Agree: I completely agree. / That's a good point. / Exactly.
Partly agree: I see your point, but… / That's true to some extent, however…
Disagree politely: I'm not sure I agree. / I see it a bit differently. / Have we considered…?
Respectful disagreement is valued in good teams. Focus on the idea, not the person.
Avoid a flat 'You are wrong.' Use 'I see it differently because…'

lessons.example:
A: We should cut the marketing budget.
B: I see your point, but I'm not sure that's the best option. Have we considered reducing travel costs instead?
speak: That's a good point.
I see your point, but I see it a bit differently.
Have we considered another option?

quiz.q: Which is a polite way to disagree?
options: I see it a bit differently.

quiz.q: 'I see your point, but…' is used to…

lessons.title: Giving updates: present perfect
lessons.summary: Report progress with 'have done', 'have already', 'haven't yet'.

sections.b:
Present perfect = have/has + past participle. Use it for results now, with no specific past time.
I've finished the draft. We've already contacted the vendor. I haven't received the data yet.
With a specific time use past simple: I finished it yesterday.
Perfect for stand-ups and status emails: 'So far we've completed 3 of 5 modules.'
Don't use present perfect with a finished time: 'I have sent it yesterday' ✗ → 'I sent it yesterday' ✓.

lessons.example: Quick update: I've completed the data cleaning, and I've already shared the first dashboard. I haven't received the sales figures yet, so the forecast is pending.
speak: I've completed the first draft.
We haven't received the data yet.
Have you already spoken to the client?

quiz.q: Complete: We ___ already contacted the vendor.

lessons.title: Speaking in meetings
lessons.summary: Join discussions, interrupt politely and keep the floor.

sections.b:
Interrupt: Sorry to interrupt, but… / Can I add something here?
Keep the floor: If I could just finish…
Bring others in: What do you think, Ana?
Return to topic: Coming back to the budget…
Many professionals stay silent in meetings. Prepare one point in advance and use these phrases to enter.
Wait for a small pause, then use a softener: 'Sorry to jump in…'

lessons.example: Sorry to interrupt, but can I add something here? I think the timeline is too tight. What do you think, Ana?
speak: Sorry to interrupt, but can I add something here?
If I could just finish my point.
Coming back to the budget, I think we need more data.

quiz.q: A polite way to interrupt is…
quiz.why: Apologise briefly, then add your point.

quiz.q: 'Coming back to the budget…' helps to…
options: Return the discussion to the topic

quiz.q: To include a quiet colleague, you can say…

lessons.title: Small talk that builds relationships
lessons.summary: Go beyond 'How are you?' with follow-up questions.

sections.b:
Safe topics: weekend, travel, food, sports, work projects, weather.
Follow-ups: Oh really? How was it? / What did you like most? / How did you get into that?
Share a little about yourself too.
Small talk before meetings builds trust. Aim for a balanced exchange: ask, listen, share, ask again.
Avoid yes/no-only questions. Ask open questions starting with How, What or Why.

lessons.example:
A: Did you do anything nice at the weekend?
B: I went trekking near Pune.
A: Oh nice! How was it? Which trail did you take?
speak: Did you do anything nice at the weekend?
Oh really? How was it?
What do you enjoy most about your job?

quiz.q: Which question keeps small talk going best?
options: What did you enjoy most about the trip?

lessons.title: Explaining a problem and solution
lessons.summary: Describe issues clearly and propose next steps.

sections.b:
Problem: The issue is that… / We're facing a problem with…
Cause: This is because… / It's caused by…
Solution: I suggest we… / One option is to… / The next step is…
Managers appreciate people who bring solutions along with problems.
Use 'suggest' + -ing or 'suggest that we': 'I suggest checking…' or 'I suggest that we check…', not 'I suggest to check'.

lessons.example: The issue is that customer complaints have increased by 20%. This is because delivery times are longer. I suggest that we add a second courier partner.
speak: The issue is that the report is delayed.
This is because the data arrived late.
I suggest that we extend the deadline by one day.

options: I suggest to check the data.

lessons.title: For and since
lessons.summary: Talk about duration with the present perfect.

sections.b:
for + period: for three years, for two hours, for a long time.
since + starting point: since 2021, since Monday, since I joined.
I've worked here for three years / since 2022.
How long have you worked here?
Interviews and introductions: 'I've been in finance for five years.'
Don't use present simple: 'I work here since 2020' ✗ → 'I've worked here since 2020' ✓.

lessons.example:
A: How long have you been with the company?
B: I've been here since 2021, so for about three years now.
speak: I've worked here for three years.
I've known her since college.
How long have you been in this role?

options: I work here since five years.
I've worked here for five years.
I worked here since five years.
I'm working here since five years.

lessons.title: Must, have to, need to
lessons.summary: Express rules, obligations and necessity.

sections.b:
must: strong obligation, often the speaker's view or written rules: You must wear your ID badge.
have to: external obligation: I have to submit the report by Friday.
need to: necessity: We need to update the software.
No obligation: don't have to / don't need to (= not necessary). Prohibition: mustn't (= not allowed).
Explaining policies and priorities clearly: 'We have to comply with the new GST rules.'
'You don't have to come' (optional) ≠ 'You mustn't come' (not allowed). This difference is important!

lessons.example: All employees must complete the security training. You don't have to do it today, but you need to finish it by the 30th.
speak: We have to submit the report by Friday.
You don't have to attend, but it's useful.
Visitors mustn't enter without a badge.

quiz.q: Complete: I ___ finish this today; my manager needs it.

lessons.title: Reported speech
lessons.summary: Tell others what someone said.

sections.b:
Direct: 'I'm busy.' → Reported: She said (that) she was busy.
Tense often moves back: am → was, will → would, can → could, have done → had done.
Questions: He asked if I could join. / She asked when the meeting was.
Requests: He asked me to send the file.
Summarising client calls and meetings: 'The client said they would approve it next week.'
Use 'said' without a person, 'told' with a person: 'She said me' ✗ → 'She told me' / 'She said' ✓.

lessons.example: Client: 'We will sign the contract next week.' → The client said they would sign the contract the following week.
speak: The client said they would sign next week.
She told me the report was ready.
He asked me to send the file again.

options: She said to me she is late yesterday.
She said me she was late.
She told me she was late.

quiz.q: 'I can help.' → He said he ___ help.

options: She asked me to call her.

lessons.title: Phrasal verbs for work
lessons.summary: Use common phrasal verbs that colleagues use every day.

sections.b:
set up (arrange/establish): set up a meeting.
follow up (on): follow up on the proposal.
carry out (do): carry out a survey.
look into (investigate): I'll look into it.
put off (postpone): put off the launch.
fill in (complete a form / replace someone): fill in for a colleague.
Phrasal verbs make your English sound natural in meetings and emails.
Some phrasal verbs separate: 'set the meeting up' / 'set it up' (not 'set up it'). With pronouns, the pronoun goes in the middle.

lessons.example: Let's set up a call with the vendor next week. I'll look into the pricing issue and follow up with you by Thursday.
speak: I'll look into it and get back to you.
Can we set up a meeting for Monday?
Let's put off the launch until next month.

lessons.title: Describing trends and charts
lessons.summary: Talk about numbers going up and down.

sections.b:
Up: rise, increase, grow, go up, climb. Down: fall, decrease, drop, decline, go down.
Speed: sharply, dramatically, steadily, slightly, gradually.
Stable: remain stable, level off, stay flat. Peak: reach a peak of…
Nouns: a sharp rise in sales, a slight drop in costs.
Presenting results: 'Revenue rose sharply in Q2, then levelled off in Q3.'
Use 'by' for the amount of change and 'to' for the final value: 'Sales increased by 10% to ₹50 crore.'

lessons.example: As you can see, revenue increased steadily from January to April, reached a peak of ₹12 crore in May, and then fell slightly in June.
speak: Sales rose sharply in the second quarter.
Costs fell by five percent to two crore rupees.
Revenue levelled off in September.

lessons.title: Making suggestions
lessons.summary: Suggest ideas naturally in meetings.

sections.b:
Why don't we + verb? / How about + -ing? / What about + -ing? / Let's + verb. / Shall we + verb? / We could + verb.
Responding: That's a good idea. / I'm not sure that will work because…
Suggestions move discussions forward without sounding bossy.
'How about' takes -ing: 'How about meet' ✗ → 'How about meeting' ✓. 'Why don't we' takes the base verb.

lessons.example:
A: We're behind schedule.
B: Why don't we split the work? How about Riya handling the testing?
A: That's a good idea. Let's do that.
speak: Why don't we split the work?
How about meeting on Thursday instead?
We could ask the client for more time.

quiz.q: Complete: How about ___ a short break?
Complete: Why don't we ___ the vendor?
Which is a polite way to reject a suggestion?
options: I'm not sure that will work because…

lessons.title: Comparing options and deciding
lessons.summary: Weigh pros and cons out loud and reach a decision.

sections.b:
Pros/cons: The advantage of Option A is… / The main drawback is… / On the one hand… on the other hand…
Weighing: Overall, I think… / The deciding factor is… / It's a trade-off between cost and speed.
Decision: Let's go with Option B.
Decision meetings need clear comparison language and a recommendation.
'On the one hand' needs 'on the other hand' to complete the idea. Don't use 'on the other side'.

lessons.example: On the one hand, Vendor A is cheaper. On the other hand, Vendor B has better support. The deciding factor is reliability, so let's go with Vendor B.
speak: The main advantage is the lower cost.
On the other hand, it's slower to set up.
Overall, I think we should go with Option B.

quiz.q: Which phrase completes 'On the one hand…'?

lessons.title: Handling complaints politely
lessons.summary: Respond to unhappy customers or colleagues calmly.

sections.b:
Listen and acknowledge: I understand your frustration. / I'm sorry to hear that.
Clarify: Could you tell me what happened? / When did you notice the problem?
Act: Let me look into this for you. / I'll get back to you by 3 pm.
Follow up: Is there anything else I can help with?
Complaints handled well can increase loyalty. Calm language de-escalates.
Avoid 'That's not my department.' Say 'Let me connect you with the right team.'

lessons.example:
Customer: My order arrived damaged!
You: I'm really sorry to hear that. Could you share a photo of the package? I'll arrange a replacement today and update you by 5 pm.
speak: I'm really sorry to hear that.
Could you tell me exactly what happened?
I'll look into it and get back to you by five.

quiz.q: The first step with a complaint is to…
Instead of 'That's not my department', say…
options: Let me connect you with the right team.

lessons.title: The passive voice for processes
lessons.summary: Describe what is done, when the doer isn't important.

sections.b:
Form: be + past participle. The invoice is approved by the manager. The data was collected last month. The report will be sent tomorrow.
Use when the action matters more than who did it, or to sound more formal.
Describing processes and reports: 'First, the request is submitted. Then it is reviewed and approved.'
Don't overuse the passive. It can sound evasive ('Mistakes were made'). Use active voice when ownership matters.

lessons.example: First, the purchase request is submitted online. It is then reviewed by the finance team, and the payment is processed within five days.
speak: The request is reviewed by the finance team.
The data was collected last month.
The report will be sent tomorrow morning.

quiz.q: Make it passive: 'The team tested the app.'
options: The app is testing by the team.
The app was tested by the team.
The team was tested the app.
The app tested by the team.
When the action matters more than the doer

quiz.q: Why can 'Mistakes were made' sound bad?

lessons.title: Linking words
lessons.summary: Connect ideas smoothly.

sections.b:
Adding: and, also, in addition, moreover.
Contrast: but, however, although, while.
Cause/result: because, so, therefore, as a result.
Sequence: first, then, after that, finally.
'Although' joins two clauses: Although sales rose, profit fell.
Linking words make your explanations structured and easy to follow.
'However' starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon) and needs a comma: 'Sales rose. However, profit fell.' Don't use 'although… but' together.

lessons.example: First, we analysed the data. Then we interviewed customers. Although most were happy, some found the app slow. Therefore, we are improving performance.
speak: Although sales increased, our profit fell.
However, we still need approval from finance.
As a result, we are changing our plan.

options: Although it rained, but we went.
However it rained but we went.

quiz.q: Complete: The plan is good. ___, it is expensive.

lessons.title: Strengths and weaknesses in interviews
lessons.summary: Answer the classic interview questions confidently.

sections.b:
Strengths: name 2-3, each with an example. 'One of my strengths is attention to detail. For example, I found a ₹2 lakh billing error last quarter.'
Weakness: be honest + show improvement: 'I used to find public speaking difficult, so I joined a speaking club and now present monthly.'
Interviewers want self-awareness and evidence, not perfect people.
Avoid clichés like 'I'm a perfectionist' or 'I work too hard'. Use a real weakness that doesn't block the job, and your improvement plan.

lessons.example: My key strength is problem-solving. For example, I automated our weekly report and saved six hours a week. One area I'm working on is delegation; I now plan tasks with my team every Monday.
speak: One of my main strengths is attention to detail.
For example, I found a billing error that saved two lakh rupees.
One area I'm working on is delegation.

options: A critical job skill you lack totally

quiz.q: Which is a cliché to avoid?

lessons.title: Presenting with signposts
lessons.summary: Guide your audience through a presentation.

sections.b:
Opening: Today I'd like to talk about… / I've divided my talk into three parts.
Moving on: Let's move on to… / Turning now to…
Highlighting: What's important here is… / As you can see from this chart…
Closing: To sum up… / The key takeaway is… / I'm happy to take questions.
Signposts help listeners follow complex information, which is essential for presenting results to leadership.
Don't read slides. Use signposts and speak to the audience.

lessons.example: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about our Q3 results. I've divided my talk into three parts: revenue, costs and next steps. Let's start with revenue.
speak: Today I'd like to talk about our quarterly results.
Let's move on to the cost analysis.
To sum up, the key takeaway is that margins improved.

quiz.q: Which phrase signals a new section?
quiz.why: 'Let's move on to…' moves to the next part.

quiz.q: 'As you can see from this chart' is used to…

lessons.title: Negotiation language
lessons.summary: Propose, counter-offer and reach agreement professionally.

sections.b:
Proposing: We'd like to propose… / How would you feel about…?
Conditional offers: If you can…, we could… / We're prepared to… provided that…
Rejecting softly: I'm afraid that's not quite what we had in mind.
Closing: So, to confirm, we've agreed on…
Use conditional language to trade concessions rather than simply giving them away.
'Provided that' and 'as long as' make offers conditional: 'We can offer 5% off, provided that you sign for two years.'

lessons.example: If you can increase the order to 500 units, we could offer a 7% discount. I'm afraid 10% isn't quite what we had in mind.
speak: How would you feel about a two-year contract?
If you can increase the volume, we could offer a discount.
So, to confirm, we've agreed on a seven percent discount.

quiz.q: Which sentence makes a conditional offer?
options: We can offer 5% off, provided that you pay in advance.
quiz.why: 'Provided that' links the concession to a condition.

quiz.q: 'That's not quite what we had in mind' is…

lessons.title: Giving constructive feedback
lessons.summary: Use the SBI model to give feedback that helps, not hurts.

sections.b:
SBI = Situation, Behaviour, Impact.
Situation: In yesterday's client call…
Behaviour: you interrupted the client twice…
Impact: which made them less open to sharing details.
Then ask: How do you see it? / What could we try next time?
Specific, behaviour-based feedback is easier to accept and act on. Use SBI for positive feedback too.
Avoid labels like 'You're careless.' Describe behaviour: 'The report had three calculation errors.'

lessons.example: In this morning's presentation, you explained the data really clearly, and the client asked fewer questions as a result. Great job!
speak: In yesterday's meeting, you explained the numbers very clearly.
The impact was that the client felt confident.
What could we try differently next time?

options: The report had three calculation errors.

quiz.q: SBI can also be used for…

lessons.title: Diplomatic language and softeners
lessons.summary: Sound polite and professional when delivering difficult messages.

sections.b:
Softeners: slightly, a bit, a little, perhaps, might.
Negative + positive word: 'not very good' → 'not ideal'; 'bad' → 'not quite what we expected'.
Past tense for politeness: I was wondering if… / I wanted to ask…
Questions instead of statements: Shouldn't we…? / Could we perhaps…?
Diplomacy matters with clients, seniors and cross-cultural teams.
Too much softening can confuse. Make sure the message is still clear.

lessons.example: Direct: 'Your price is too high.' → Diplomatic: 'I'm afraid the price is a little higher than we expected. Could there be some flexibility?'
speak: I'm afraid the price is a little higher than we expected.
I was wondering if we could move the deadline.
Could we perhaps look at another option?

quiz.q: Make it diplomatic: 'The report is bad.'
options: The report isn't quite what we expected.

lessons.title: Conditionals for proposals and scenarios
lessons.summary: Discuss possibilities and consequences.

sections.b:
First conditional (real future): If we launch in May, we will beat the competition.
Second conditional (hypothetical): If we had a bigger budget, we would hire two more people.
Third conditional (past regret): If we had tested earlier, we would have found the bug.
Scenario planning, proposals and retrospectives all use conditionals.
Don't use 'will' in the if-clause: 'If it will rain' ✗ → 'If it rains' ✓.

lessons.example: If we automate invoicing, we'll save about 20 hours a month. If we had more data, we would build a forecasting model.
speak: If we automate this process, we'll save a lot of time.
If we had a bigger budget, we would hire more people.
If we had tested earlier, we would have found the issue.

options: If we finished early, we will leave.
If we finish early, we will leave.
If we will finish early, we will leave.
quiz.why: First conditional: If + present, will + verb.

lessons.title: Handling questions and Q&A
lessons.summary: Answer questions confidently, even when you don't know.

sections.b:
Welcome: That's a great question. / Thanks for asking.
Clarify: If I understand correctly, you're asking about…
Buy time: Let me think about that for a second.
Don't know: I don't have that figure with me, but I'll get back to you by tomorrow.
Never guess numbers in front of senior people. Promise a follow-up and deliver it.
Don't overuse 'That's a great question'. Vary your responses.

lessons.example:
Q: What's the churn rate for enterprise clients?
A: If I understand correctly, you're asking about the last quarter? I don't have that exact figure with me, but I'll send it to you by tomorrow.
speak: Thanks for asking. Let me think about that for a second.
If I understand correctly, you're asking about the costs.
I don't have that figure with me, but I'll get back to you by tomorrow.

quiz.q: You don't know the answer in a meeting. Best response?
options: I don't have that figure now, but I'll get back to you by tomorrow.
quiz.why: Honest plus a clear follow-up builds credibility.

quiz.q: 'If I understand correctly, you're asking about…' helps to…
To buy time before answering, say…
options: Let me think about that for a second.

lessons.title: Business collocations
lessons.summary: Use the word combinations native speakers expect.

sections.b:
make: a decision, a profit, a mistake, progress, an offer.
do: business, research, a good job, your best.
take: action, responsibility, a risk, notes.
meet: a deadline, expectations, targets.
raise: a concern, funds, prices.
Collocations make your English sound fluent and precise: 'We need to take action to meet the deadline.'
Common error: 'do a decision' ✗ → 'make a decision' ✓; 'make business' ✗ → 'do business' ✓.

lessons.example: We made good progress this quarter and met all our targets. However, we need to take action on costs. I'd like to raise a concern about supplier delays.
speak: We need to make a decision by Friday.
The team met every deadline this quarter.
I'd like to raise a concern about the budget.

quiz.q: Complete: Did we ___ our sales targets?

lessons.title: Formal and informal register
lessons.summary: Match your tone to the person and situation.

sections.b:
Informal → Formal:
get → receive/obtain; help → assist; ask → enquire; need → require; start → commence; fix → resolve; tell → inform.
'Can you send it?' → 'Would you be able to send it?'
'Thanks a lot' → 'Thank you very much' / 'I appreciate your help'.
Clients, senior leaders and official communication need a more formal register; teammates usually informal.
Too formal with close colleagues can sound cold; too casual with clients can sound unprofessional. Mirror the other person's style.

lessons.example:
Informal: Hey, can you fix the login issue? Thanks!
Formal: Dear Mr Rao, could you please help us resolve the login issue? I appreciate your support.
speak: Would you be able to send the report today?
I appreciate your help with this.
We will inform you once the issue is resolved.

options: Would you be able to send it?

quiz.q: A good rule for register is to…

lessons.title: Delivering bad news
lessons.summary: Share difficult information honestly and kindly.

sections.b:
Prepare the listener: I'm afraid I have some bad news. / Unfortunately…
Be clear: The launch will be delayed by two weeks.
Explain briefly: This is because the testing found critical bugs.
Next steps: Here's what we're doing to fix it…
Empathy: I know this is disappointing.
Leaders are trusted when they deliver bad news early, clearly and with a plan.
Don't hide the main message in long explanations. State it within the first two sentences.

lessons.example: I'm afraid I have some bad news. The product launch will be delayed by two weeks because testing found critical bugs. I know this is disappointing. We've added two engineers and will update you every Friday.
speak: I'm afraid I have some bad news.
Unfortunately, the launch will be delayed by two weeks.
Here's what we're doing to fix the problem.

quiz.q: When should the main bad news come?
What builds trust after bad news?

lessons.title: Persuading with data
lessons.summary: Combine numbers and stories to convince people.

sections.b:
Use: The data shows that… / According to our analysis… / This represents a 20% improvement… / To put that in perspective…
Make numbers meaningful: '₹50 lakh a year, which is about the cost of four engineers.'
End with an ask: So I recommend that we…
Leaders respond to clear numbers linked to business impact.
Too many numbers confuse. Choose 1-3 key figures and explain why they matter.

lessons.example: Our analysis shows that 30% of support tickets are password resets. That's around 2,000 hours a year, roughly the time of one full-time employee. So I recommend that we introduce self-service resets.
speak: Our analysis shows that costs have risen by twenty percent.
To put that in perspective, it's the cost of four new hires.
So I recommend that we automate this process.

quiz.q: How many key numbers should you usually highlight?

options: Make a number meaningful by comparison

quiz.q: A persuasive data talk should end with…

lessons.title: Must be, might be, can't be
lessons.summary: Make logical guesses about the present and past.

sections.b:
Present: must be (almost certain), might/may/could be (possible), can't be (almost certainly not).
She isn't answering. She must be in a meeting.
Past: must have + past participle: He must have forgotten. / They can't have received it yet.
Discussing possibilities in problem-solving: 'The server can't be down; others can access it. It might be your VPN.'
The opposite of 'must be' (deduction) is 'can't be', not 'mustn't be'.

lessons.example:
A: Payment hasn't arrived.
B: It can't have been sent yet; the bank is closed today. It might arrive tomorrow.
speak: She must be in a meeting; she isn't answering.
It might be a problem with your internet.
They can't have received the email yet.

quiz.q: The opposite of 'He must be at home' (deduction) is…
options: He doesn't must be at home.

quiz.q: Complete: The file is missing. Someone ___ it.
quiz.why: Past deduction: must have + past participle.

lessons.title: Advanced phrasal verbs
lessons.summary: Sound natural in project and negotiation talk.

sections.b:
iron out (resolve small problems): iron out the details.
push back (resist / postpone): push back on the deadline.
follow through (complete what you promised).
bring up (mention a topic). come up with (create an idea).
rule out (exclude). sign off on (approve).
These appear constantly in corporate meetings and emails.
'Push back' has two meanings: resist ('The client pushed back on price') and postpone ('We pushed the launch back a week'). Check the context.

lessons.example: We still need to iron out a few details before the CFO signs off. Legal pushed back on two clauses, and we can't rule out a short delay.
speak: Let's iron out the details before Friday.
The client pushed back on the price.
We need the CFO to sign off on the budget.

options: Think of an idea or plan
Write a signature on a card

lessons.title: Networking conversations
lessons.summary: Start, sustain and end conversations at events.

sections.b:
Openers: Hi, I'm Yash. What brings you here today? / How do you know the host? / What did you think of the keynote?
Sustain: That's interesting, how did you get into that?
Exit gracefully: It's been great talking to you. Shall we connect on LinkedIn? / I'll let you go and mingle.
Events, conferences and alumni meets create opportunities if you're comfortable chatting.
Don't hard-sell immediately. Build connection first, then follow up within 48 hours with a personal note.

lessons.example:
A: Hi, I'm Yash, I work in fintech. What brings you here?
B: I'm Anjali, I lead data at a logistics startup.
A: Oh, interesting! How are you using AI there?
speak: Hi, I'm Yash. What brings you here today?
That's interesting, how did you get into that field?
It's been great talking to you. Shall we connect on LinkedIn?

quiz.q: When should you follow up after meeting someone?

options: Excuse me, someone better is here.
I'll let you go and mingle. Great talking to you!

lessons.title: From small talk to business
lessons.summary: Move smoothly from friendly chat to the agenda.

sections.b:
Transition phrases: Shall we get started? / Anyway, I know you're busy, so… / Moving on to why we're here… / Right, let's turn to the proposal.
Recap purpose: As discussed, today we want to…
Good meetings start warm but move to business without awkwardness.
Don't skip small talk completely in relationship-focused cultures (common in India, Japan, the Middle East). Read the room.

lessons.example: Great to hear about your trip to Goa! Anyway, I know you're busy, so shall we get started? As discussed, today we'd like to agree on the Q3 timeline.
speak: Anyway, I know you're busy, so shall we get started?
Right, let's turn to the proposal.
As discussed, today we'd like to agree on the timeline.

quiz.q: Which phrase signals a move to business?
In relationship-focused cultures, skipping small talk can seem…

lessons.title: Cause and effect
lessons.summary: Explain why things happened and what followed.

sections.b:
Cause: due to + noun (due to delays), because of + noun, owing to, as a result of, because + clause.
Effect: as a result, consequently, therefore, which led to, resulting in.
Example: Due to higher fuel costs, margins fell, which led to a price increase.
Root-cause explanations and business reviews depend on clear cause-effect language.
'Due to' and 'because of' take a noun phrase: 'due to it rained' ✗ → 'due to the rain' / 'because it rained' ✓.

lessons.example: Due to supply shortages, production slowed in April. As a result, we missed two deliveries, which led to a penalty of ₹3 lakh.
speak: Due to supply shortages, production slowed down.
As a result, we missed two deliveries.
This led to a penalty of three lakh rupees.

options: Due to the rain, we stayed.
Due to it rained, we stayed.
Because of it rained, we stayed.

lessons.title: Video-call language
lessons.summary: Run and join virtual meetings smoothly.

sections.b:
Tech: You're on mute. / Can everyone see my screen? / You froze for a second. / I'll drop the link in the chat.
Turn-taking: Go ahead, Priya. / Sorry, after you. / Let me just jump in here.
Closing: I'll share the recording and notes. / Thanks, everyone, have a good day.
Most cross-city and global work happens on video calls. Smooth language keeps calls efficient.
When two people talk at once, say 'Sorry, go ahead' and let them speak. Name people when asking for input; silence on calls is common.

lessons.example: Hi everyone, can you all see my screen? Great. Rohan, you're on mute. Before we start, I'll drop the agenda in the chat.
speak: Can everyone see my screen?
Sorry, you're on mute.
I'll drop the link in the chat.

quiz.q: If two people speak at once, a polite response is…
Why name people when asking for input on calls?
options: Silence is common; naming invites participation

lessons.title: Summarising and paraphrasing
lessons.summary: Show understanding and keep everyone aligned.

sections.b:
Paraphrase: So what you're saying is… / If I understand correctly, you mean… / In other words…
Summarise: To sum up, we've agreed three things… / The key points are… / Let me recap.
Summaries prevent misunderstandings, especially in multicultural teams and with clients.
A good summary is shorter than the original and focuses on decisions and actions, not every detail.

lessons.example: If I understand correctly, you need the dashboard by Friday, but the forecast can wait until next week. Let me recap: dashboard Friday, forecast next Wednesday, and I'll send updates daily.
speak: If I understand correctly, you need it by Friday.
In other words, the budget is fixed.
Let me recap the key points.

options: Check understanding in your own words

lessons.title: Persuasive framing
lessons.summary: Frame ideas around what your audience cares about.

sections.b:
Lead with the benefit, not the feature: 'This saves each analyst 5 hours a week' beats 'This has automation features.'
Use contrast: Not only… but also…
Use the audience's priorities: 'Given our focus on margins, this option…'
Leaders decide based on outcomes, risk and cost. Frame proposals in those terms.
Avoid overselling. Credibility comes from balanced arguments: mention a risk and how you'll manage it.

lessons.example: Given our focus on improving margins, I'd recommend automating reconciliation. Not only would it save 200 hours a quarter, but it would also reduce errors. The main risk is implementation time, which we can manage with a phased rollout.
speak: Given our focus on margins, I'd recommend this option.
Not only would it save time, but it would also reduce errors.
The main risk is cost, which we can manage with a phased rollout.

quiz.q: Which opening is most persuasive to a cost-focused CFO?
options: This saves ₹20 lakh a year in manual work.
quiz.why: Frame around the audience's priority: cost.

quiz.q: Leading with the benefit means saying…
options: It saves each analyst 5 hours a week.

quiz.q: Why mention a risk in a persuasive pitch?
options: To show balance and build credibility

lessons.title: Business idioms and expressions
lessons.summary: Understand and use common corporate idioms naturally.

sections.b: Touch base = briefly contact. Ballpark figure = rough estimate. On the same page = in agreement. Get the ball rolling = start. Low-hanging fruit = easy wins. Back to square one = start again. Think outside the box = be creative.
Idioms are common in global companies. Understand them all; use a few naturally.
Don't overuse idioms with non-native speakers. Clarity wins over sounding fancy.

lessons.example: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the project? Let's touch base on Friday to make sure we're all on the same page. Let's start with the low-hanging fruit.
speak: Could you give me a ballpark figure?
Let's touch base on Friday.
Let's start with the low-hanging fruit.

quiz.why: A ballpark figure is an approximate number.

lessons.title: Hedging: expressing certainty precisely
lessons.summary: Show exactly how sure you are, which is a sign of a careful professional.

sections.b:
High certainty: clearly, undoubtedly, the data shows.
Medium: it appears that, it seems likely, this suggests.
Low: it's possible that, may/might, arguably.
Useful: To the best of my knowledge… / Based on the available data…
In analysis and reports, overclaiming damages credibility. Hedging shows rigour.
Don't hedge everything; it can sound unsure. Match the language to the evidence.

lessons.example: Based on the available data, it appears that the decline is seasonal. However, it's possible that the new competitor has also had an impact.
speak: Based on the available data, it appears that sales are recovering.
This suggests that the campaign was effective.
It's possible that other factors also played a role.

lessons.title: Chairing and leading meetings
lessons.summary: Run meetings that start on time, stay on track and end with actions.

sections.b:
Open: Let's get started. The purpose of today's meeting is…
Manage: Let's park that for now. / We're running short of time, so…
Invite: Rohan, we haven't heard from you yet.
Close: Let's recap the action points. Priya will… by Friday.
Leading meetings well is one of the most visible leadership skills.
Always end with owners and deadlines: 'Who will do what by when?'

lessons.example: Let's get started. The purpose of today's meeting is to agree on the Q4 budget. We have 30 minutes. Let's park the hiring question for now and come back to it next week.
speak: Let's get started. The purpose of today's meeting is to agree on the budget.
Let's park that for now and come back to it later.
Let's recap the action points before we finish.

options: Action points with owners and deadlines
Need to speed up or prioritise

lessons.title: Interview stories with STAR
lessons.summary: Answer behavioural questions with clear, memorable stories.

sections.b:
STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result.
S: Set the scene briefly. T: Your responsibility. A: What YOU did (use 'I', not 'we'). R: The measurable outcome and what you learned.
Most interviews include 'Tell me about a time when…' questions. STAR keeps answers to about 2 minutes.
Spend most of the time on Action and Result. Quantify results where possible.

lessons.example: Situation: Our month-end closing took 10 days. Task: I was asked to speed it up. Action: I automated three reconciliations using Python. Result: Closing time fell to 6 days, and the method was rolled out to two other teams.
speak: I was responsible for reducing the month-end closing time.
I automated three reconciliations using Python.
As a result, closing time fell from ten days to six.

quiz.q: In STAR, which part should get the most time?
quiz.why: Interviewers care most about what you did and achieved.

lessons.title: Pronunciation: stress and intonation
lessons.summary: Sound clearer by stressing the right syllables and words.

sections.b:
Word stress: DE-ve-lop → de-VE-lop; PHO-to-graph → pho-TO-gra-phy; a-NA-ly-sis; e-CO-no-my.
Sentence stress: stress key information words. 'We need the REPORT by FRIDAY.'
Intonation: falling for statements, rising for yes/no questions.
Correct stress makes you easier to understand than a perfect accent. Clarity is the goal.
Common stress mistakes: say 'de-VE-lop' not 'DE-ve-lop', 'ho-TEL' not 'HO-tel', and 'COM-pa-ny' not 'com-PA-ny'.

lessons.example: Listen and repeat with the speaker button. Exaggerate the stressed syllable at first, then make it natural.
speak: We need to develop a new strategy for the company.
The analysis shows that the economy is growing.
Could you send me the report by Friday?

quiz.why: de-VE-lop: stress on the second syllable.

lessons.title: Inversion for emphasis
lessons.summary: Add power to key messages with inverted structures.

sections.b:
Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject:
Never have we seen such strong demand.
Rarely do clients complain about quality.
Not only did we cut costs, but we also improved quality.
Only after testing will we launch.
At no point did we compromise on safety.
Inversion appears in speeches, formal presentations and executive writing for emphasis.
Use sparingly, once or twice in a talk. Overuse sounds theatrical. Remember the auxiliary: 'Never we have seen' ✗ → 'Never have we seen' ✓.

lessons.example: Not only did the team deliver on time, but they also came in 10% under budget. Rarely have I seen such commitment.
speak: Never have we seen such strong demand.
Not only did we cut costs, but we also improved quality.
Only after testing will we launch the product.

quiz.q: Complete: Rarely ___ such a good result.

lessons.title: Cleft sentences for focus
lessons.summary: Highlight what matters most in a sentence.

sections.b:
What-clefts: What we need is more time. / What surprised me was the speed.
It-clefts: It was the pricing that lost us the deal. / It's the team that deserves credit.
All-clefts: All we need is approval.
Cleft sentences direct attention: great for presentations and feedback.
Stress the focus word when speaking: 'What we NEED is TIME.'

lessons.example: It wasn't the product that lost us the deal; it was the delivery timeline. What we need now is a faster onboarding process.
speak: What we need is a clear decision.
It was the pricing that lost us the deal.
All we need now is the CFO's approval.

options: What we need is more time.

quiz.q: 'It was the team that deserves credit' emphasises…

lessons.title: Discourse markers that sound fluent
lessons.summary: Guide listeners through complex reasoning.

sections.b:
Conceding: Admittedly… / Granted… / Having said that…
Contrasting: That said… / Even so… / By contrast…
Adding: What's more… / Not to mention…
Generalising: By and large… / On the whole…
Returning: Be that as it may… / At any rate…
These markers make you sound thoughtful and fluent in discussions and presentations.
'Having said that' introduces a contrast with what you just said, not agreement.

lessons.example: Admittedly, the new system cost more than planned. Having said that, it has already cut processing time by half. On the whole, I'd call it a success.
speak: Admittedly, the project ran over budget.
Having said that, the results are excellent.
On the whole, I'd call it a success.

lessons.title: The 60-second elevator pitch
lessons.summary: Explain who you are or what your idea is, in a minute.

sections.b:
Structure: Hook (problem) → Who you are/what you do → Value (proof/numbers) → Ask.
'Most SMEs spend 20 hours a month on invoicing. I'm Yash; I build tools that cut that to two. Our pilots saved 15 clients ₹3 lakh each. I'd love 20 minutes to show you a demo.'
Useful at networking events, with senior leaders in a lift, and in interviews ('Tell me about yourself').
Don't list your whole CV. Be specific, use one number and end with a clear ask.

lessons.example: 'Tell me about yourself' → 'I'm a finance professional who loves automating boring work. In my last role I automated monthly reporting, saving 40 hours a month. Now I'm looking to bring that to a fintech team like yours.'
speak: Most small businesses waste twenty hours a month on invoicing.
Our pilots saved each client three lakh rupees.
I'd love twenty minutes to show you a demo.

quiz.q: An elevator pitch should end with…
How long should an elevator pitch take?

lessons.title: Managing stakeholder expectations
lessons.summary: Set, reset and protect expectations professionally.

sections.b:
Setting: Realistically, we can deliver by… / To manage expectations, the first version will only include…
Resetting: In light of the new requirements, we'll need to revisit the timeline.
Protecting: I'd rather under-promise and over-deliver.
Trade-offs: If we add X, we'll need to drop Y or move the date.
Projects fail when expectations drift. Clear language prevents disappointment.
Avoid vague promises like 'We'll try our best to finish soon.' Give specific dates, scope and assumptions.

lessons.example: To manage expectations, version one will cover only payments. Realistically, reporting will follow in March. If we add reporting now, we'd need to move the launch by three weeks.
speak: To manage expectations, the first version is limited.
If we add this feature, we'll need to move the date.
I'd rather under-promise and over-deliver.

options: Set realistic expectations and exceed them

quiz.q: A good way to handle a new request is to…
options: Explain the trade-off with scope or time

quiz.q: Which is a vague promise to avoid?
options: We'll try our best to finish soon.

lessons.title: Mixed conditionals
lessons.summary: Connect past causes with present results, and vice versa.

sections.b:
Past condition → present result: If we had invested earlier, we would be market leaders now.
Present condition → past result: If I were more organised, I wouldn't have missed the deadline.
Use to reflect on decisions and their consequences.
Retrospectives and strategic discussions: 'If we had hired a data team last year, we'd have better forecasts today.'
Keep the time logic clear: the 'if' part and the result part refer to different times.

lessons.example: If we had automated reconciliation last year, we wouldn't be working weekends now. And if our data were cleaner, we would have spotted the issue earlier.
speak: If we had invested earlier, we would be leading the market now.
If our data were cleaner, we would have spotted the issue.
If I had joined sooner, I'd know the system better now.

options: If we had planned better, we would be relaxed now.
If you heat ice, it melts.

quiz.q: Complete: If I ___ the email, I would know the answer now.
quiz.why: Past perfect for the past condition.

options: Reflecting on how past decisions affect the present

lessons.title: Giving feedback upwards
lessons.summary: Share honest input with your manager or seniors respectfully.

sections.b:
Ask permission: Would it be helpful if I shared some feedback on the review meeting?
Focus on impact and shared goals: I noticed that… and I think it might affect…
Offer a suggestion: One idea could be…
Show support: I want this project to succeed as much as you do.
Organisations improve when people can speak up. Respectful upward feedback builds your credibility.
Choose timing and privacy carefully: one-on-one, not in front of others. Speak about specific situations, not personality.

lessons.example: Would it be helpful if I shared an observation about yesterday's meeting? I noticed the team went quiet when the deadline was announced. I think they're worried about workload. One idea could be to review priorities together.
speak: Would it be helpful if I shared some feedback?
I noticed that the team went quiet when the deadline was announced.
One idea could be to review priorities together.

quiz.q: Where should upward feedback usually happen?

options: Would it be helpful if I shared some feedback?

lessons.title: Connected speech
lessons.summary: Understand and sound natural with linking, weak forms and contractions.

sections.b:
Linking: consonant + vowel join: 'turn_off' → 'tur-noff', 'look_at_it' → 'loo-ka-tit'.
Weak forms: 'to' → /tə/, 'and' → /ən/, 'can' → /kən/ (in 'I can come').
Contractions: I'll, we've, wouldn't, should've.
Gonna/wanna are informal speech, not for writing.
Understanding fast native speech in calls and videos requires knowing these patterns, and using some makes you sound fluent.
Don't stress every word equally. Stress content words (nouns, main verbs) and reduce function words (to, a, of, and).

lessons.example: Listen to 'What are you going to do about it?' In fast speech: 'Whaddaya gonna do aboudit?' Practise the slow version first, then speed up.
speak: What are you going to do about it?
I'll look at it after lunch.
We should've checked it earlier.

quiz.q: In 'I can come', 'can' is usually pronounced…

options: Content words like nouns and main verbs

lessons.title: Strong adjective and adverb collocations
lessons.summary: Add precision and intensity naturally.

sections.b:
Adverb + adjective: highly unlikely, deeply concerned, fully aware, strongly recommend, widely recognised, bitterly disappointed.
Adjective + noun: sharp increase, heavy losses, fierce competition, sound judgment, steep learning curve, tight deadline.
These collocations make reports and presentations sound polished and confident.
Some combinations sound wrong: 'very unlikely' is fine but 'highly unlikely' is stronger; 'strong rain' ✗ → 'heavy rain' ✓.

lessons.example: We are fully aware of the tight deadline and fierce competition. However, it is highly unlikely that we will miss the launch. I strongly recommend we proceed.
speak: We are fully aware of the tight deadline.
It is highly unlikely that we will miss the launch.
I strongly recommend that we proceed.

lessons.title: Talking about numbers precisely
lessons.summary: Say figures, approximations and changes correctly.

sections.b:
Approximations: roughly, approximately, just under/over, around, in the region of.
Changes: doubled, tripled, a twofold increase, halved, fell by a third.
Fractions/percentages: three-quarters, 0.5 percentage points (not 0.5%).
Indian vs international: 1 lakh = 100,000; 1 crore = 10 million.
Finance and business reviews require exact numerical language, especially with global audiences.
If interest rises from 5% to 6%, that is 1 percentage point, but a 20% increase. Mixing these up is a classic error.

lessons.example: Revenue doubled to just over ₹10 crore, that's about $1.2 million. Our margin improved by 2 percentage points, to roughly 18%.
speak: Revenue doubled to just over ten crore rupees.
Margins improved by two percentage points.
That's roughly one point two million dollars.

lessons.title: Executive communication: bottom line up front
lessons.summary: Lead with the conclusion. Senior people want the answer first.

sections.b:
BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) / Pyramid Principle: start with the main message, then 2-3 supporting points, then details only if asked.
'My recommendation is X. Three reasons: A, B, C.'
Executives have limited time. Structured, concise answers signal leadership readiness.
Avoid building up to the conclusion with long background. If interrupted, they should already have your answer.

lessons.example: Bottom line: we should acquire FinCo. Three reasons: it adds 2 million users, it fills our lending gap, and the price is 20% below comparable deals. I can walk through the numbers if helpful.
speak: My recommendation is that we expand into Tier-2 cities.
There are three reasons: demand, lower costs and less competition.
I'm happy to go into the details if that's helpful.
