quiz.why: Bottom Line Up Front: give the answer first.

quiz.q: If an executive interrupts you, they should already have…

lessons.title: Difficult conversations and conflict
lessons.summary: Stay calm and constructive in tense situations.

sections.b:
Acknowledge: I can see why you're frustrated. / I understand this is a concern.
I-statements: I felt concerned when the deadline was missed.
Shared goal: We both want this project to succeed.
Move forward: What would a good solution look like for you?
Handling conflict well protects relationships and is a key leadership competency.
Avoid 'you always' or 'you never'. They trigger defensiveness.

lessons.example: I understand you're frustrated about the delays, and I share that concern. We both want this launch to succeed. Could we look at what's blocking the team and agree on a realistic date?
speak: I can see why you're frustrated, and I share that concern.
We both want this project to succeed.
What would a good solution look like for you?

options: I understand this is a concern for you.

quiz.q: 'We both want this to succeed' highlights…

lessons.title: Precise vocabulary
lessons.summary: Replace vague words with precise, powerful ones.

sections.b:
Instead of 'good' → effective, robust, compelling, viable.
Instead of 'bad' → flawed, unsustainable, counterproductive.
Instead of 'change' → revise, overhaul, streamline, pivot.
Instead of 'big' → substantial, significant, considerable.
Instead of 'show' → demonstrate, indicate, reveal.
Precise words make you sound expert and reduce misunderstanding.
Don't use complex words just to impress. Choose the word that is most exact.

lessons.example: The pilot demonstrated a significant reduction in costs, but the current process is unsustainable at scale. We need to streamline approvals.
speak: The results demonstrate a significant improvement.
The current process is unsustainable at scale.
We need to streamline the approval process.

quiz.q: Best replacement for 'The plan is good' in a business case?
quiz.why: 'Viable' means workable and realistic, which is precise.

quiz.q: A precise word for 'change a process to make it simpler' is…

lessons.title: Rhetorical techniques
lessons.summary: Make key messages memorable with classic techniques.

sections.b:
Rule of three: faster, cheaper, safer.
Contrast: It's not about working harder; it's about working smarter.
Rhetorical question: What would happen if we did nothing?
Repetition: We will learn. We will adapt. We will win.
Great speeches and town halls use these techniques to inspire and stick in memory.
Use one or two techniques per talk. Too many sound theatrical.

lessons.example: What would happen if we did nothing? Our competitors would move faster, serve customers better and win. It's not about cutting costs; it's about investing wisely.
speak: Our solution is faster, cheaper and safer.
It's not about working harder; it's about working smarter.
What would happen if we did nothing?

quiz.q: 'Faster, cheaper, safer' is an example of…
'It's not about X; it's about Y' is an example of…
How many rhetorical techniques per talk is wise?

lessons.title: Cross-cultural communication
lessons.summary: Adapt your style to global colleagues.

sections.b:
Direct cultures (e.g. Netherlands, Germany) value frank, explicit messages. Indirect cultures (e.g. Japan, India) often rely on context and politeness.
Also differs: attitudes to hierarchy, time and saying 'no'.
Tip: In global calls, be explicit about decisions and next steps.
Global teams succeed when people adapt rather than assume everyone communicates like them.
'Yes' doesn't always mean agreement in indirect cultures; it can mean 'I hear you'. Confirm with specific questions.

lessons.example: To make sure we're aligned: we're agreeing to deliver phase one by 15 March, and Lena's team will own testing. Does anyone see a risk with that date?
speak: To make sure we're aligned, let me summarise the decisions.
Does anyone see a risk with that date?
Please feel free to share any concerns, even after the call.

quiz.q: In global calls, it's best to make decisions…

lessons.title: Impromptu speaking with PREP
lessons.summary: Answer unexpected questions with a clear structure.

sections.b:
PREP = Point, Reason, Example, Point.
Point: state your view. Reason: why. Example: evidence or story. Point: restate to close.
Pause for 2 seconds before answering. Silence looks thoughtful.
Useful when a senior leader suddenly asks 'What do you think?' in a meeting.
Don't ramble. When you restate your point, stop talking.

lessons.example: Point: I think we should invest in training. Reason: our biggest delays come from skill gaps. Example: last quarter, three projects slipped because only one person knew the new tool. Point: so training is the fastest way to speed up delivery.
speak: I think we should invest in training.
The reason is that skill gaps cause most of our delays.
So training is the fastest way to speed up delivery.

quiz.q: Before answering an unexpected question, it's good to…
In PREP, after the Example comes…

lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos
lessons.summary: Use Aristotle's three appeals to persuade any audience.

sections.b:
Ethos: credibility (experience, values, trust). Pathos: emotion (stories, hopes, fears). Logos: logic (data, reasoning, evidence).
The strongest arguments balance all three, adjusted for the audience: finance leaders want more logos; teams often need more pathos.
Pitches, town halls and negotiations all benefit from deliberately combining the three.
Pathos without logos can feel manipulative; logos without pathos can feel cold. Ethos is earned through consistency.

lessons.example: Ethos: 'Having run operations for ten years…' Pathos: 'Our nurses are exhausted, working double shifts…' Logos: 'Automating scheduling saves 1,200 hours a year.'
speak: Having led operations for ten years, I've seen this pattern before.
Our nurses are exhausted and working double shifts.
Automation would save twelve hundred hours a year.

quiz.q: Too much pathos without logos can seem…

lessons.title: Humour and lightness at work
lessons.summary: Use light humour to build rapport, without risk.

sections.b:
Safe humour: self-deprecating, situational ('Well, the projector clearly has opinions today'), light irony.
Risky humour: about religion, politics, gender, appearance or anyone's mistakes.
Timing: after rapport is built, not during bad news.
Appropriate humour reduces tension, makes you memorable and humanises leaders.
Humour and irony don't always translate across cultures. With global teams, keep it simple and kind.

lessons.example: As the slides refused to load: 'Well, this is my live demonstration of why we need the new IT budget.' Everyone laughed, and the point landed.
speak: Well, the projector clearly has opinions today.
I promise the next slide is less painful than this one.
That's my live demonstration of why we need the new budget.

quiz.q: Which humour is safest at work?
quiz.why: Laugh at yourself or the situation.

quiz.q: Why be careful with irony in global teams?
options: It may not translate across cultures

lessons.title: Crisis communication
lessons.summary: Speak with clarity and calm when things go wrong.

sections.b:
Framework: Acknowledge → Explain what you know (and don't) → Action → Next update.
'We're aware of the outage affecting payments. We don't yet know the cause. Our engineers are working on it, and we'll update you within 30 minutes.'
Empathy: We understand how frustrating this is.
In crises, people need honesty, speed and a sense that someone is in control.
Never speculate or blame publicly. Say what you know, admit what you don't and commit to the next update time.

lessons.example: We're aware that some customers cannot complete UPI payments. We've identified the issue with a partner bank and are working on a fix. We understand how frustrating this is, and we'll update you by 2 pm.
speak: We're aware of the issue and are working on it urgently.
We don't yet know the cause, but we'll update you within thirty minutes.
We understand how frustrating this is.

quiz.q: The first step in crisis communication is to…
What should you say if you don't know the cause yet?
options: Say you don't know yet and when you'll update
It shows control and reduces anxiety

lessons.title: Briefing the board or investors
lessons.summary: Communicate with senior decision-makers concisely and confidently.

sections.b:
Structure: headline → 3 key messages → risks → the decision needed.
Language: 'The headline is…' / 'Three things to highlight…' / 'The key risk is… and we're mitigating it by…' / 'We're seeking approval for…'
Anticipate questions; prepare a backup appendix.
Board time is short; directors value clarity, candour about risks and a crisp ask.
Don't drown the board in operational detail. Know the numbers cold and answer 'I'll come back to you' if unsure.

lessons.example: The headline is that we're ahead of plan on revenue but behind on hiring. Three things to highlight… The key risk is attrition, which we're mitigating with retention bonuses. Today we're seeking approval for a ₹20 crore expansion.
speak: The headline is that we're ahead of plan on revenue.
The key risk is attrition, and we're mitigating it with retention bonuses.
Today we're seeking approval for the expansion.

quiz.q: A board briefing should start with…

options: Candour about risks and a clear ask

quiz.q: If you don't know an answer, say…
options: I'll come back to you with that

lessons.title: Idioms that native speakers use
lessons.summary: Understand idiomatic English in meetings and media.

sections.b:
Move the goalposts: change the rules unfairly.
Bite the bullet: accept something unpleasant.
The elephant in the room: an obvious problem nobody mentions.
A blessing in disguise: something bad that turns out good.
Cut corners: do something poorly to save time/money.
Go the extra mile: do more than expected.
Global colleagues and leaders use idioms often. Understanding them avoids confusion; using a few adds colour.
Use idioms in their fixed form: 'the elephant in the room', not 'the elephant inside the room'.

lessons.example: Let's address the elephant in the room: the budget. We'll have to bite the bullet and delay hiring, but we won't cut corners on quality.
speak: Let's address the elephant in the room.
We'll have to bite the bullet and delay hiring.
The team really went the extra mile this quarter.

options: Unfairly change the rules or targets
Do poor work to save time or money
Something bad that turns out good

lessons.title: Style-shifting for any audience
lessons.summary: Adjust vocabulary, length and tone instantly.

sections.b:
Same message, three styles:
Executive: 'We'll miss Q3 by 5%; recovery plan in place.'
Team: 'We're a bit behind, here's how we'll catch up together.'
Customer: 'Your order will arrive two days later than planned. We're sorry and have waived the delivery fee.'
Masters of communication flex style for executives, peers, customers and juniors while keeping the message accurate.
Ask before speaking: Who is listening? What do they care about? How much time do they have? What action do I want?

lessons.example: Explain a server outage to (1) the CTO: root cause and fix; (2) sales: impact on clients and what to tell them; (3) customers: apology and when it will work.
speak: We'll miss the quarterly target by five percent, but a recovery plan is in place.
We're a bit behind, so here's how we'll catch up together.
We're sorry for the delay and have waived the delivery fee.

options: Changing tone and detail for the audience while keeping the message

quiz.q: Before speaking, a key question is…
options: What does this audience care about?

lessons.title: Moderating panels and events
lessons.summary: Host discussions with poise and keep them on track.

sections.b:
Opening: Welcome, everyone. Today's theme is… I'm delighted to introduce our panellists…
Guiding: Let me bring in Anita on that. / Building on that point… / In the interest of time, let's move to…
Audience: Let's open the floor to questions.
Closing: Please join me in thanking our panellists.
Hosting events and panels raises your visibility and is a mark of senior communication skill.
Prepare questions, but listen and follow up on interesting answers. Keep speaking time balanced across panellists.

lessons.example: Building on Ravi's point about regulation, let me bring in Anita: how is your bank preparing? … In the interest of time, let's open the floor to questions.
speak: Welcome, everyone. I'm delighted to introduce our panellists.
Building on that point, let me bring in Anita.
Please join me in thanking our panellists.

options: Ask Anita to enter the room

quiz.q: A good moderator keeps speaking time…

lessons.title: Reading between the lines
lessons.summary: Understand what polite English phrases really mean.

sections.b:
Native speakers (especially British) often understate:
'With respect…' ≈ I disagree.
'That's an interesting idea' ≈ maybe not good.
'I'll bear it in mind' ≈ I probably won't do it.
'Quite good' ≈ okay, not great.
'Not bad' ≈ good.
Misreading polite signals causes surprises in global teams. Confirm meaning when stakes are high.
When unsure, ask a clarifying question: 'Just to check, would you like us to change the approach?'

lessons.example: Client: 'That's a brave proposal.' (Translation: risky; they're unlikely to approve.) You: 'Thank you. Just to check, do you have concerns we should address?'
speak: Just to check, would you like us to change the approach?
With respect, I see the risks differently.
Could you tell me what concerns you about the proposal?

quiz.q: 'I'll bear it in mind' often means…
options: Probably not going to act on it

quiz.q: When polite phrases are ambiguous, you should…

lessons.title: Giving a keynote-style talk
lessons.summary: Inspire an audience with a memorable message.

sections.b:
Structure: Big idea in one sentence → Story that shows the problem → 3 insights → Call to action → Callback to the opening story.
Techniques: pause after big lines, vary pace and volume, use concrete images, repeat the key phrase.
Keynotes, conference talks and leadership speeches shape reputation and influence.
Rehearse the opening and closing word for word; the middle can be more flexible. Time yourself; running over is disrespectful to the audience.

lessons.example: Opening: 'Ten years ago, a farmer in Nashik showed me his phone and said: "This is my bank." Today, I want to talk about how technology makes everyone a participant in the economy…' Closing: 'So the next time you see a phone, remember: it might be someone's bank.'
speak: Today, I want to share one big idea with you.
Let me tell you a short story.
So the next time you see a phone, remember, it might be someone's bank.

quiz.q: A keynote should be built around…

options: Returning to the opening story at the end

quiz.q: Which parts should you rehearse word for word?

lessons.title: Your personal speaking mastery plan
lessons.summary: Keep improving long after the lessons end.

sections.b:
Mastery habits: record and review one talk a month; shadow great speakers for 10 minutes daily; keep a vocabulary journal of 5 precise words a week; get feedback from a trusted colleague; speak up once in every meeting.
Measure: fillers per minute, pace (~140-160 words/min) and clarity.
The best communicators treat speaking as a lifelong craft. Small daily practice compounds.
Don't aim for a 'perfect accent'. Aim for clarity, confidence and connection, which matter far more for success.

lessons.example: My plan: Monday, shadow a TED talk for 10 minutes. Wednesday, speak up first in the team meeting. Friday, record a 2-minute update and count my fillers. Monthly, ask my manager for one piece of feedback.
speak: I will speak up at least once in every meeting.
Clarity and confidence matter more than accent.
Every week I'll record myself and review it.

quiz.q: A comfortable speaking pace is about…
What matters more than a 'perfect accent'?

options: Repeating after a speaker in real time

lessons.title: Day 1: Decode the job and the company
lessons.summary: Great answers start with knowing exactly what they want.

sections.b:
Read the job description (JD) like a detective. Highlight: (1) must-have skills, (2) nice-to-have skills, (3) repeated words (they show priorities), (4) the problems this role solves.
Research the company: products, customers, recent news, annual report highlights, competitors, culture (Glassdoor/AmbitionBox, LinkedIn posts of employees).
Make a 'match table': JD requirement → your proof (project, number, story).
Build a one-page cheat sheet: company in 3 lines, 5 JD keywords, 5 matching proofs, 2 recent news items, and why you're excited.
Don't memorise the company's 'About us' page. Interviewers want to hear how YOU connect to their problems.

lessons.example:
JD says: 'Experience in financial reporting and automation.'
Your proof: 'At my last company I automated the monthly MIS report in Excel and Python, cutting preparation time from 3 days to 4 hours.'
speak: I've researched your recent expansion into tier-two cities.
This role needs strong reporting skills, and that's my core strength.
I'm excited because this role combines finance and technology.
lessons.action: Create your match table for one real job posting today.

options: JD requirements mapped to your proof
quiz.why: It turns your experience into evidence.

quiz.q: Repeated words in a JD usually show…

options: Products, customers, recent news and culture

lessons.title: Day 2: 'Tell me about yourself'
lessons.summary: Nail the most common opening question in 60-90 seconds.

sections.b:
Use Present → Past → Future:
Present: who you are now and your current role/impact.
Past: 1-2 highlights that led here (with numbers).
Future: why this role is the logical next step.
Keep it professional and relevant; personal details only if they support the story.
Write your answer (150-200 words), then say it aloud 5 times. Record yourself and cut anything that doesn't help you get THIS job.
Don't recite your CV line by line or start with your school and hometown. Lead with your current professional identity.

lessons.example: 'I'm a finance professional with four years in FP&A at a fintech company. Currently I lead monthly reporting for a ₹200 crore business. Before that, I automated our MIS reports, saving 40 hours a month. Now I want to bring that mix of finance and automation to a larger team, which is why this role at your company excites me.'
speak: I'm a finance professional with four years of experience in planning and analysis.
Most recently, I automated our monthly reports and saved forty hours a month.
That's why I'm excited about this role.
lessons.action: Write and record your 'Tell me about yourself' answer. Keep it under 90 seconds.

quiz.why: Start with who you are now.

options: Why this role is your logical next step

lessons.title: Day 3: Build your STAR story bank
lessons.summary: Prepare 6 stories that answer 80% of behavioural questions.

sections.b:
STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result (+ Learning).
Prepare 6 stories: (1) a big achievement, (2) a failure/mistake, (3) conflict or disagreement, (4) leadership/initiative, (5) working under pressure/deadline, (6) learning something new fast.
Each story: 90-120 seconds, mostly Action and Result, with numbers.
Fill a table: story name, S, T, A (3 bullet actions using 'I'), R (number), learning. Then map each story to likely questions.
Say 'I' for your actions. 'We did…' hides your contribution, and interviewers hire individuals.

lessons.example:
Question: 'Tell me about a time you worked under pressure.'
S: Quarter-end close, two team members on leave. T: Deliver the board pack in 3 days. A: I prioritised critical schedules, automated two reconciliations and set twice-daily check-ins. R: Delivered a day early with zero audit comments. L: I now build buffers into close calendars.
speak: The situation was a tight quarter-end deadline.
I automated two reconciliations to save time.
As a result, we delivered a day early with zero errors.
lessons.action: Write your 6 STAR stories in a table with one number in each result.

quiz.q: In STAR, most time should go to…
How many core stories are recommended?
Which word shows your contribution best?

lessons.title: Day 4: Strengths and weaknesses
lessons.summary: Answer honestly, with evidence and growth.

sections.b:
Strength = skill + proof + relevance to the job. Pick 2-3 strengths that match the JD.
Weakness = a real but non-critical gap + what you're doing about it + progress so far.
Avoid fake weaknesses ('I'm a perfectionist').
Write 3 strengths with a one-line story each, and 1 weakness with your improvement plan and evidence of progress.
Never pick a weakness that is a core requirement of the role, e.g. 'attention to detail' for an audit job.

lessons.example:
Strength: 'Turning messy data into decisions. For example, I built a dashboard that helped sales cut discount leakage by 2%.'
Weakness: 'I used to say yes to too many requests. Now I prioritise with my manager every Monday, and my on-time delivery improved to 98%.'
speak: One of my key strengths is turning data into decisions.
For example, my dashboard helped reduce discount leakage by two percent.
I'm working on delegation, and I now plan tasks with my team every Monday.
lessons.action: Write and practise your strength and weakness answers aloud three times.

options: Proof and relevance to the job

quiz.q: Which weakness would hurt an auditor candidate?

lessons.title: Day 5: Why this company, why this role, why leave?
lessons.summary: Show genuine motivation without negativity.

sections.b:
Why this company: 1-2 specific reasons (product, mission, growth, culture) + how you'll contribute.
Why this role: the skills you'll use and grow.
Why leave: focus on moving TOWARD something (growth, scope, learning), never bad-mouth your employer.
Draft three 30-second answers. Include one fact from your research in 'Why this company'.
Never say 'my manager is bad' or 'I just need more money' as your main reason. Negativity is a red flag.

lessons.example: 'Your company is expanding lending to small businesses, and I've spent three years in SME credit analytics. I'd love to help scale that. I'm looking to move because I've learned a lot in my current role, and I'm ready for broader responsibility in a faster-growing team.'
speak: I'm excited by your expansion into small-business lending.
I've learned a lot in my current role, and I'm ready for broader responsibility.
This role lets me use my analytics skills at a larger scale.
lessons.action: Write all three answers for one target company and say them aloud.

quiz.q: The best 'why leave' answers focus on…

options: A specific fact and how you'll contribute

quiz.why: Interviewers worry you'll do it again.

lessons.title: Day 6: Teamwork and conflict questions
lessons.summary: Show you can work with difficult people and situations.

sections.b:
Common questions: 'Tell me about a conflict with a colleague.' 'How do you handle disagreement with your manager?'
Framework: describe the disagreement neutrally → how you listened → how you found common ground (data, shared goal) → outcome → relationship after.
Pick a real conflict story. Remove blame words. Add the line 'I wanted to understand their perspective, so I…'
Avoid stories where you 'won' and the other person 'lost'. Interviewers look for collaboration, not victory.

lessons.example: 'A sales head wanted to change the forecast every week. Instead of arguing, I asked what worried him. It was missing early signals. We agreed on a weekly flash report and a monthly forecast. Forecast accuracy improved, and we still work closely.'
speak: I wanted to understand their perspective first.
We agreed on a solution that met both our goals.
We still have a strong working relationship.
lessons.action: Write your conflict story using neutral language and practise it.

quiz.q: A good conflict story ends with…
options: A shared solution and a good relationship

quiz.q: A key behaviour to show is…
Which word should you avoid in conflict stories?

lessons.title: Day 7: Leadership, ownership and failure
lessons.summary: Prove you take initiative, even without a title.

sections.b:
Leadership = influencing outcomes: leading a project, mentoring, fixing a broken process, speaking up.
Failure question: choose a real failure, own it, explain what you learned and what you do differently now.
Ownership phrases: 'I took responsibility for…', 'I noticed X and proposed Y.'
Prepare one leadership story and one failure story. In the failure story, at least 40% should be about learning and change.
Don't pick a fake failure or blame others. 'My failure was that my team didn't…' is not ownership.

lessons.example: 'I underestimated the time needed for a data migration and we missed the first deadline. I told my manager immediately, re-planned with the team and we delivered two weeks later. Since then I add a 20% buffer and do a risk check before committing dates.'
speak: I took responsibility for fixing the process.
I told my manager immediately and created a new plan.
Since then, I always add a buffer to my estimates.
lessons.action: Write your failure story and highlight the learning part.

quiz.q: Leadership without a title can include…
options: Fixing a broken process on your own initiative

quiz.q: In a failure story, focus heavily on…

lessons.title: Day 8: The technical / functional round
lessons.summary: Explain your expertise clearly and handle tough questions.

sections.b:
Revise the fundamentals of your field (for finance: three statements, ratios, NPV/IRR, WACC, working capital, budgeting, variance analysis; use Gyaanly's finance path!).
Explain simply: definition → why it matters → example from your work.
If you don't know: say what you do know, how you'd find out, and don't bluff.
List 15 likely technical questions from the JD. Answer each in 3 sentences: definition, importance, example.
Don't bluff. 'I haven't used that tool, but I've used a similar one and I learn fast; for example…' is far better than a wrong answer.

lessons.example:
Q: 'What's the difference between profit and cash flow?'
A: 'Profit is revenue minus expenses on an accrual basis; cash flow is actual cash in and out. A company can be profitable but short of cash, for example if customers pay late. At my last company we tracked DSO weekly for exactly that reason.'
speak: Profit and cash flow are different, and here's why it matters.
Let me give you an example from my work.
I haven't used that tool, but I've used a similar one.
lessons.action: Answer 5 technical questions aloud using definition, importance, example.

options: Definition, why it matters, and an example

quiz.q: If you don't know an answer, you should…
options: Share what you know and how you'd find out

quiz.q: Where can you revise finance fundamentals?

lessons.title: Day 9: Case questions and structured thinking
lessons.summary: Solve business problems out loud.

sections.b:
Many interviews include a mini case: 'Profits fell 20%, why?' or a guesstimate: 'How many cups of tea are sold in Mumbai daily?'
Approach: clarify the question → state assumptions → structure (issue tree: revenue vs costs; population × % × frequency) → calculate → sanity-check → recommend.
Practise 2 cases: one profitability case, one guesstimate. Speak your thinking aloud.
Don't jump to answers. Interviewers grade your structure and communication more than the final number.

lessons.example: 'Profits fell 20%. Let me clarify: over what period, and are competitors affected too? I'll split profit into revenue (price × volume) and costs (fixed and variable). Let me start with revenue: has our price or volume changed?'
speak: Let me clarify the question first.
I'll break profit into revenue and costs.
Based on these assumptions, my estimate is about two million cups a day.
lessons.action: Solve one guesstimate aloud in under 5 minutes and record it.

quiz.q: The first step in a case is to…
Profit can first be split into…

lessons.title: Day 10: AI, tools and digital skills questions
lessons.summary: Show you use AI wisely, a hot topic in every interview now.

sections.b:
Expect: 'How do you use AI in your work?' 'What tools are you good at?' 'How do you check AI output?'
Answer with: a specific workflow → time or quality gain → how you verify → where you deliberately don't use AI (confidential data, final judgment).
Write two examples of AI or automation in your work with numbers, plus your verification method.
Avoid 'I use ChatGPT for everything' as well as 'I never use AI'. Both sound risky. Show judgment.

lessons.example: 'I use AI to draft variance commentary from our MIS data. It cuts drafting time by about half. I always check every number against the source file and edit the business explanation myself. I never paste confidential client data into public tools.'
speak: I use AI to create first drafts, then I verify every number.
It reduced my report preparation time by half.
I never share confidential data with public tools.
lessons.action: Prepare your 'How do you use AI?' answer using the Human Edge path ideas.

options: A workflow, the gain, and how you verify

quiz.q: A responsible AI habit to mention is…
Why mention where you don't use AI?
options: It shows judgment and risk awareness

lessons.title: Day 11: Body language, voice and video interviews
lessons.summary: Look and sound confident, in person and online.

sections.b:
In person: firm (not crushing) handshake, eye contact, upright posture, open hands, smile.
Voice: moderate pace (≈140-160 words/min), pause before answering, lower pitch at the end of statements.
Video: camera at eye level, light in front of you, plain background, test audio, look at the camera when speaking, keep notes off-screen.
Record a 2-minute mock answer on video. Review posture, eye contact, filler words ('um', 'like') and lighting.
Looking at your own video image instead of the camera makes you seem distracted. Look at the lens when making key points.

lessons.example: Before a video interview: 'Test link 15 minutes early, laptop charged, phone on silent, water nearby, JD and STAR notes on a sticky note behind the camera.'
speak: Thank you for having me today.
That's a great question; let me think for a moment.
Could you please repeat the last part? The audio cut out.
lessons.action: Set up your video interview space and do a 2-minute test recording.

quiz.q: A good speaking pace is about…
Before answering a hard question it's fine to…

lessons.title: Day 12: Questions to ask the interviewer
lessons.summary: End strong and learn whether the job fits you.

sections.b:
Always have 3-5 questions. Good ones:
• 'What does success look like in the first 6 months?'
• 'What are the biggest challenges for this team right now?'
• 'How does the team use data/AI in decision-making?'
• 'What do you enjoy most about working here?'
• 'What are the next steps in the process?'
Avoid asking about salary or leave in the first round unless they raise it.
Write 5 questions tailored to your target company and rank your top 3.
'No, I don't have any questions' signals low interest. Always ask at least two.

lessons.example:
Interviewer: 'Do you have any questions for us?'
You: 'Yes, thank you. What would success look like for this role in the first six months? And what's the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?'
speak: What does success look like in the first six months?
What are the biggest challenges for the team right now?
What are the next steps in the process?
lessons.action: Prepare your 5 questions and memorise the top 3.

options: How many leaves do I get?
What does success look like in 6 months?
Can I work from home daily?

quiz.q: When is it usually fine to discuss salary?
options: When the employer raises it or at the HR/offer stage

lessons.title: Day 13: HR round and salary negotiation
lessons.summary: Discuss pay confidently and professionally.

sections.b:
Research the range (AmbitionBox, Glassdoor, LinkedIn Salary, peers). Know your current CTC breakdown, notice period and minimum acceptable number.
When asked expectations: give a researched range, anchored slightly high, linked to value.
Negotiate the full package: fixed, variable, joining bonus, ESOPs, notice buyout, learning budget, flexibility.
Write your target range, walk-away number and 3 value points (achievements with numbers). Practise the script aloud.
Don't give a number with no research, and don't accept immediately. 'Thank you, could I have a day to review the full offer?' is professional.

lessons.example: 'Based on my research for similar roles and the impact I've delivered, such as automating reporting that saved 40 hours a month, I'm looking for a range of ₹18 to 21 lakh fixed. I'm open to discussing the overall package.'
speak: Based on my research, I'm looking for a range of eighteen to twenty-one lakh.
I'm open to discussing the overall package.
Thank you. Could I have a day to review the offer?
lessons.action: Fill in your salary research sheet and rehearse your expectation answer.

options: A researched range linked to your value

quiz.q: Besides fixed pay, you can negotiate…
options: Joining bonus, ESOPs, notice buyout, learning budget

quiz.q: A professional response to an offer is…
options: Thank them and ask for time to review

lessons.title: Day 14: Full mock interview
lessons.summary: Put everything together under realistic pressure.

sections.b:
Run a 30-45 minute mock: tell me about yourself → 2 behavioural (STAR) → 2 technical → 1 case/guesstimate → why us → your questions.
Use a friend, mentor or an AI interviewer (paste the JD and ask it to act as the hiring manager and give scored feedback).
Score yourself 1-5 on: structure, clarity, evidence (numbers), confidence, relevance.
Record the mock. Watch it once and list the 3 biggest improvements. Re-answer those three questions.
Don't just read answers. Interviewers can tell. Use bullet keywords, not scripts, so you sound natural.

lessons.example: AI interviewer prompt: 'Act as the hiring manager for this JD. Ask me 8 interview questions one at a time, wait for my answer, then give a score out of 5 and one improvement for each.'
speak: Thank you for the opportunity to interview today.
Let me walk you through a relevant example.
I'd like to summarise why I'm a strong fit.
lessons.action: Complete one full recorded mock interview and write your top 3 fixes.

options: Intro, behavioural, technical, case and your questions
To spot habits you can't notice live

quiz.q: Better than a full script is…

lessons.title: Day 15: Interview day, follow-up and next steps
lessons.summary: Finish strong and handle any outcome professionally.

sections.b:
Day before: confirm time/location/link, plan the route, prepare documents (CV copies, ID, certificates), outfit, sleep well.
On the day: arrive 10-15 minutes early (online: log in 5 minutes early), review your cheat sheet, breathe.
After: send a thank-you email within 24 hours referencing one specific discussion point.
Outcome: if rejected, ask politely for feedback; if offered, review the full offer before accepting.
Write your thank-you email template and your interview-day checklist.
Don't stop applying while waiting for one result. Keep momentum with multiple opportunities.

lessons.example:
Subject: Thank you, Financial Analyst interview
'Dear Ms Rao, thank you for your time today. I enjoyed discussing how your team plans to automate monthly reporting, and I'm even more excited about contributing my experience there. Please let me know if I can share anything else. Best regards, Yash'
speak: Thank you for your time today.
I enjoyed our discussion about automating monthly reporting.
I look forward to hearing about the next steps.
lessons.action: Send yourself the thank-you email template and tick off your checklist. You've completed the 15-day course! 🎉

quiz.q: When should you send a thank-you email?
If rejected, a professional step is…
